Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marta Ivanov (Redwood SE), James Miller (Sunriver Head of ML), Sara Lopez (Sunriver Infra), Tom Nguyen (Sunriver CTO), Nina Patel (Product)

Auto-generated sections (optional):
Summary: see metadata field above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check, can you all see my slides?
[00:04] James Miller: Yep, I can see them. Looks good.
[00:08] Alex Chen: Awesome. I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account and Priya is our SE who will walk through Optimize and the batching + KV cache cost model, um Marta is here too for any follow ups on configs.
[00:18] Priya Rao: Hey hi, thanks. So today we'll do a short recap of what Redwood Optimize recommends for high-throughput generation workloads, specifically prefix/KV cache strategies and continuous batching, and then map that to Sunriver's traffic pattern.
[00:30] Sara Lopez: Quick thing, our main constraint is p95 latency under 150ms for interactive flows, but we also have large background scoring jobs so cost matters a lot.
[00:40] Tom Nguyen: And we need everything in our VPC, with KMS-managed keys, SOC2 compliance, audit logs — basic enterprise stuff.
[00:50] Priya Rao: Totally, we'll cover private options and the diffs with hosted. For the Optimize part: the two levers we usually tune are batching (how many requests we pack together) and KV/prefix caching (how much of the prompt or conversation state we keep in GPU memory to avoid recomputation).
[01:10] James Miller: Can you start with a quick micro example — like 1k requests per minute, avg seq len 120 tokens, what numbers change?
[01:20] Priya Rao: Sure. So for your example the biggest wins come from KV cache if you have repeated prefixes — e.g., templates or system prompts that are identical across requests. If you can cache the prefix (we call it prefix cache) you only do the heavy attention work once per prefix, then subsequent requests reuse the KV cache which is ~X ms per call instead of full forward of model.
[01:40] James Miller: X ms meaning?
[01:42] Priya Rao: Sorry, rough numbers: full forward for a 70B-ish open model on a V100-equivalent might be ~200-250ms per chunk, but with KV cache reuse the per-request incremental is more like 30-50ms, depending on sequence length and kernel performance. Those are ballpark and depend on quantization and kernels.
[02:05] Marta Ivanov: Also continuous batching reduces per-token cost by up to 2.5x in typical steady load by filling GPU work — but it can increase tail latency if you set batch timeouts too high.
[02:20] Sara Lopez: So what's Redwood's recommendation to balance p95 latency vs cost?
[02:24] Priya Rao: We usually pick a target latency SLO and then tune the batch window and max batch size. For 150ms p95 we might set max batch size lower and a small micro-batch window like 8-12ms, plus aggressive prefix caching. That gets you close, cost will be higher than aggressive batching but you'll hit latency.
[02:42] Tom Nguyen: What about Ded— dedicated capacity vs hosted? We want VPC so we're leaning Private but need to understand the economics.
[02:50] Alex Chen: Right, hosted is easiest and cheapest for bursty, but if you need VPC and commit-level throughput, Dedicated or Private gives predictable unit cost. In our cost model spreadsheet (link in chat) we show per-token unit cost delta between hosted and dedicated for different commit levels.
[03:08] James Miller: Can you share that again?
[03:10] Alex Chen: Yep — deck: https://redwood.ai/quick-deck/optimize-batching-kv and spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Rw-EXAMPLE (shared with view). That spreadsheet has the scenarios we walked through.
[03:26] [00:03:30] Priya Rao: Back to KV details — Redwood's prefix cache stores KV states in RAM/GPU depending on config; small prefixes we keep in GPU to avoid PCIe roundtrips. For larger contexts we offer hybrid caching and automatic eviction policies. It's tuned by TTL and space budget.
[03:48] James Miller: How stable is it under model rollouts — like if we push a new model version do caches invalidate?
[03:54] Priya Rao: Yes, cache keys include model version and quantization fingerprint, so rollout of new model will create new cache entries. We provide warmup APIs to pre-warm the cache for key prefixes though.
[04:08] Sara Lopez: KMS integration — you mentioned keys for private. We need HSM-backed keys and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[04:16] Marta Ivanov: We support KMS/HSM via customer-managed keys and can forward audit logs via syslog or splunk forwarder. We also expose per-request audit trails in Console.
[04:28] [00:04:30] James Miller: Cool. On the cost model — what are the knobs? Batching, cache hit rate, model latency, and quantization. Anything else?
[04:38] Priya Rao: Also request heterogeneity: if you have lots of short requests mixing with long ones, batching efficiency drops. And KV cache hit rate is huge — going from 0% to 60% cache hits can reduce token compute costs by ~40% in our examples.
[04:56] Tom Nguyen: Any pitfalls customers run into?
[04:58] Priya Rao: Misconfigured TTLs — keeping too many KV entries increases memory pressure and eviction thrashing, that kills perf. Also mixing stateful chat with stateless scoring in the same worker pool can reduce cache locality. We recommend separate routes/pools for scoring vs chat.
[05:16] James Miller: For our product, about 70% of calls are templated responses with a 20-token variable, 30% are freeform chat. Seems like cacheable prefixes are high.
[05:26] Priya Rao: That's a great fit for prefix cache. If you can surface the template IDs we can do deterministic cache keys and get very high hit rates.
[05:34] Alex Chen: A note on measurement — we usually run a small benchmark with your actual prompt set. Priya, can you talk about the benchmark we propose?
[05:40] Priya Rao: Sure — run 1k requests across representative seq lengths, measure p50/p95 latency, throughput, and cache hit breakdown. We'll instrument logs to show token counts, cache hits, batch fill, and GPU utilization. That'll feed into the cost model sheet to project monthly spend at X qps.
[06:02] [00:06:00] Sara Lopez: How invasive is instrumentation? We prefer not to ship PII out of our VPC.
[06:08] Priya Rao: For Private deployments everything stays in your VPC; we recommend masked prompt sets for benchmark if needed. For Hosted we do anonymized telemetry.
[06:18] James Miller: Slight transcription note — you mentioned continuous batching, what's the difference vs micro-batching?
[06:24] Marta Ivanov: Continuous batching is our runtime technique that constantly aggregates tokens across in-flight requests (KV-aware). Micro-batching is a simpler fixed interval. Continuous gives better utilization for steady streams.
[06:36] Tom Nguyen: Ok good. Let's look at numbers — can you walk through a sample cost scenario?
[06:40] Priya Rao: I'll pull a simple scenario from the sheet: Scenario A: 1k rps peak, avg seq 120 tokens, 60% prefix cache hit. With aggressive batching (high batch size) unit cost ~0.8X baseline; with latency SLO 150ms we dial batching down and cost becomes ~1.4X baseline — exact numbers in sheet.
[07:00] James Miller: Baseline meaning OpenAI-style hosted?
[07:03] Alex Chen: Baseline in sheet is raw per-token compute cost on Redwood default config. We also show comparative rows for typical vendor pricing to give context.
[07:12] [00:07:20] Sara Lopez: How much does quantization help here? We currently run int8 on our in-house models.
[07:18] Priya Rao: Quantization reduces memory and kernel cost — int8 will reduce model compute time by ~30-50% depending on hardware and model. But there are quality tradeoffs; we include eval checks in Optimize to flag regressions.
[07:34] James Miller: We can't afford quality regressions for customer-facing flows. How do you guard?
[07:38] Priya Rao: We run eval suites on samples and will gate rollout if perplexity/accuracy thresholds fail. Also recommend A/B canary rollouts with traffic split and automatic fallback. That's in Console rollouts.
[07:52] Alex Chen: Also, in Dedicated you can pin older model for a subset of traffic during rollout.
[07:58] [00:08:00] Tom Nguyen: Regarding network — do you support colocated deployments with our on-prem data center?
[08:04] Marta Ivanov: Yes, Private can be deployed in your on-prem rack or in your cloud VPC. For on-prem we provide an air-gapped package and offline attestation for compliance-heavy customers.
[08:16] Sara Lopez: Good. A bit on the cache — what about eviction strategy? LRU? TTL? Size-based?
[08:22] Priya Rao: It's hybrid: TTL + LRU + size budget. We expose configuration for prioritizing prefixes vs full conversations. For your workload we'd recommend small TTLs for conversational state (to free mem) but indefinite or long-lived entries for stable templates.
[08:38] [00:08:40] James Miller: If we have multiple app servers hitting the same Dedicated cluster, is cache shared?
[08:44] Priya Rao: Yes — the cache is in the serving tier. All requests routed to the same pool can benefit from shared KV entries. Smart routing can route cache-friendly traffic to warmed pools.
[08:56] Tom Nguyen: That routing — is it automatic or does it require config?
[08:59] Alex Chen: It's policy-driven. You can set routing by model, by route, by customer segment. We can set warm pools for heavy templates.
[09:08] [00:09:10] Sara Lopez: Any gotchas with GPUs and large KV sizes? We saw OOMs in earlier trials with another vendor.
[09:16] Marta Ivanov: We monitor and have adaptive eviction and can spill to host memory for less critical entries. But yes, pushing KV beyond physical GPU memory will increase PCIe thrash unless you have NVLink or GPU direct storage. We recommend sizing pool with headroom.
[09:34] James Miller: Back to the benchmark — what's the minimum we need to prove value?
[09:38] Priya Rao: A 1k request synthetic run with your prompts across 10 minutes is usually enough to estimate savings and latency trends. We'll want sequence length histograms and cacheability labels.
[09:50] Alex Chen: We'll also include a short perf harness for you to run internally if you prefer not to expose prompts.
[09:58] [00:10:00] Nina Patel: Curious on ops — once live how do we observe cache hit rates and batch stats?
[10:04] Priya Rao: Console has per-route dashboards showing cache hit %, avg batch size, token breakdown, GPU utilization, and per-token cost. You can set alerts on p95 latency and cache dropoffs.
[10:18] James Miller: That's useful. For compliance we need logs for every request — can that be redacted?
[10:24] Marta Ivanov: Yes, request logs can be redacted or token counts only; we support field-level redaction and PII masking before logs leave the VPC.
[10:36] [00:10:40] James Miller: Any customers in finance doing similar?
[10:42] Alex Chen: Yes, several: Aurora Finance, Mariner Payments, and Novapayments — we've run KV-heavy deployments with similar SLOs. We can share anonymized case studies.
[10:54] Tom Nguyen: Competitors — you mentioned PlatformX earlier, how do you compare on batching and cache?
[10:58] Priya Rao: PlatformX has a simpler micro-batching model; Redwood's continuous batching plus KV-aware routing tends to give better steady-state utilization and better cost at scale. But PlatformX may be faster to get started for simple workloads.
[11:12] [00:11:20] James Miller: Ok, let's talk POC scope and timeline. We want to validate p95 <150ms on interactive plus run cost projection for 100M tokens/month.
[11:24] Alex Chen: Recommended POC: 2-week engagement: week 1 run benchmark and configure caching/batching; week 2 analyze and optimize — Priya will recommend config changes and we iterate.
[11:36] James Miller: Budget/commit?
[11:38] Alex Chen: We can run the benchmark on hosted or in your dev VPC with a short trial credit; cost for dedicated sizing will depend on commit. We'll include estimated commit tiers in the spreadsheet.
[11:48] [00:11:50] Sara Lopez: For security review we'll need whitepapers & SOC2 report.
[11:54] Marta Ivanov: I'll share our SOC2 report, architecture diagrams, and the security checklist after the call.
[12:02] Priya Rao: Quick demo — I'll flip to a live Console view (screen share) to show the per-route cache metrics and the cost model slider.
[12:08] [00:12:10] [screen sharing noise] Priya Rao: Here is a demo tenant — route A is chat with prefix caching enabled, you can see cache hit rate toggle and a simulated cost breakdown. If you bump cache hits to 80% the projected monthly compute drops significantly in the right pane.
[12:28] James Miller: Nice visual. Can you export the config?
[12:31] Priya Rao: Yep, you can export YAML for route config and we can pre-generate terraform for Dedicated.
[12:38] Tom Nguyen: Any specific infra limits — GPUs per node, max batch size?
[12:42] Marta Ivanov: Depends on instance; we typically cap batch size to avoid OOMs. For 80GB A100s you can push bigger batches; for smaller GPUs we tune smaller max batches.
[12:54] [00:12:55] Sara Lopez: One more question — we use a home-grown reranker that calls models for top-k scoring, can we mix reranking workers with chat workers?
[13:04] Priya Rao: You can, but we recommend separate worker pools for rerankers because they have different token profiles and caching characteristics. Reranking benefits less from prefix cache but can benefit from model variants quantized for throughput.
[13:18] James Miller: What's the recommended fallback policy if the cache server or pool is down?
[13:22] Alex Chen: Automatic fallback to a warm hosted pool or to lower-capacity Dedicated nodes; Redwood supports multi-tier routing with circuit breaker thresholds.
[13:32] [00:13:35] Priya Rao: Ok wrapping up technical part — I'll summarize recommended starting config for Sunriver: 1) enable prefix cache for template routes with TTL 72 hours, 2) separate route/pool for reranking, 3) batch window 10ms, max batch size tuned to hit p95 target, 4) pre-warm cache with warmup API before full rollout.
[13:56] James Miller: That sounds reasonable. Any expected cost uplift from those settings vs naive aggressive batching?
[14:02] Priya Rao: Expect cost 15-40% higher than aggressive batching depending on SLO. But with high cache hits you'll often net savings vs naive because compute per-request drops dramatically. The sheet has scenario lines.
[14:18] [00:14:20] Alex Chen: Next steps recap: Alex will share spreadsheet & deck, Priya will run benchmark and share scripts, James to share prompts and seq distribution, Marta to send SOC2 & security docs. We'll target POC kickoff next Tuesday (2026-04-28) pending your internal OK.
[14:38] Nina Patel: Sounds good. Also please include instructions to run the perf harness inside our VPC — we prefer that path.
[14:44] Priya Rao: Will do, we have a dockerized harness and a terraform module. We'll include step-by-step.
[14:52] [00:14:55] James Miller: Any final questions?
[14:56] Tom Nguyen: One small nit — can we get an estimate for warm pool memory needs per template?
[15:00] Marta Ivanov: We'll include a rough sizing table in the spreadsheet: avg KV size per prefix * entries * headroom -> GPU memory estimate. We'll size with 30% headroom.
[15:12] Alex Chen: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with artifacts.
[15:16] James Miller: Thanks all.
[15:18] Nina Patel: Thanks.
[15:20] [00:15:22] End of recording

Notes on transcription: occasional auto-caption errors (e.g., Redwood Optimize transcribed as "red wood optimize" in places), speaker overlaps, and timestamps are approximate.
